entities.name: Atlantic Records
entities.label: Institution
entities.summary:
Atlantic Records, founded in 1947 in New York City by Ahmet Ertegün (a Turkish diplomat's son with an extraordinary ear for Black American music) and Herb Abramson, is one of the most historically significant record labels in American music history — credited with pioneering rhythm and blues, soul, and rock and roll recording from the late 1940s through the 1970s, and launching the careers of Ray Charles, Aretha Franklin, Led Zeppelin, and hundreds of other defining artists.

Ahmet Ertegün's Atlantic was distinguished by its founder's genuine love for and knowledge of Black American music, unusual among record label executives of the era. Atlantic's early roster included Ruth Brown, the Clovers, Joe Turner, and Ray Charles — whose Atlantic recordings from 1952-1959 defined the R&B/soul synthesis. The 1967 signing of Aretha Franklin — who had failed to breakthrough at Columbia Records — and the immediate recognition that producer Jerry Wexler and Atlantic's approach (combined with Muscle Shoals studio musicians) could unlock her genius produced the definitive recordings of her career.

Atlantic's expansion into rock began with the Cream, Led Zeppelin, and Crosby, Stills, Nash & Young in the late 1960s. The label was acquired by Warner-Seven Arts in 1967 (becoming part of what eventually became WMG) while maintaining editorial independence. Modern Atlantic has been home to Coldplay, Bruno Mars, Ed Sheeran, Cardi B, and many contemporary acts. The label's heritage — from Ray Charles and Aretha Franklin through Led Zeppelin to Bruno Mars — makes it one of the most musically significant institutions in 20th-century American culture.
